text:
When Johnson came to set Shakespeare above the dramatists of his own age, he rested the preference upon a single ground, and he stated it with his customary firmness: "Nothing can please many, and please long, but just representations of general nature." (Johnson 1765) The persons of the lesser playwrights, as he saw them, were cut to the fashions of a particular town and a particular season; they spoke the idiom of a coterie, and acted upon motives which depended on customs long since abandoned; and when the customs passed away, the persons passed with them. Shakespeare's characters are of another kind. They are moved by passions which every reader has felt in himself or watched in others; their manners belong to no one court, no one street, no one generation; what is local in them is the dress and the phrasing, and the heart beneath is common to all mankind. Hence a reader who knows nothing whatever of the theatre for which the plays were written may open them and recognise, without any labour of learning, what he finds there. A father's rage at an ungrateful daughter, a son's grief for a dead father, a husband's jealousy worked up out of a handkerchief: these still read as true.

Johnson put the matter in a sentence which has been often quoted and seldom weighed: "Shakespeare has no heroes; his scenes are occupied only by men" (Johnson 1765). He meant it as praise. Other dramatists, in his judgment, lifted their persons above the common measure; they gave them sentiments which no one ever felt, and language which no one ever used; and so they bartered the reader's belief for his astonishment. Shakespeare's people speak as the reader himself would have spoken, had he stood where they stand. Their words come out of the occasion, and the occasion is one which he can readily imagine for himself.

Does this hold where the story quits the world we know? It holds even there. A ghost may walk the battlements, or witches may meet upon a heath; but the men who see them talk as frightened men, or doubtful men, or ambitious men commonly talk. The action rises above life; the dialogue keeps to its level. Horatio, confronted with the Ghost, does not declaim. He asks it plainly what it is, and why it has come—much as any of us would.

Johnson had no wish to praise Shakespeare by the measure of his own age, and he distrusted the praise which any single age bestows. Fashion admires what flatters it; and one generation may be pleased with a writer for reasons which the next will think trivial, or will not understand at all. The only test he would allow was duration. A work which has been read and valued through many changes of manners and of opinion must owe its hold upon us to something more than the accident of its first reception. By this test, he held, Shakespeare's case was already decided. He had been dead a century and a half; the language had altered, the stage had altered, and the taste of critics had swung from one doctrine to another; yet the plays were still acted, still read, still quoted, by men who knew nothing of the circumstances which first produced them. Johnson gave the matter a figure of his own: "The stream of time, which is continually washing the dissoluble fabricks of other poets, passes without injury by the adamant of Shakespeare." (Johnson 1765) The poets who had shared his stage had worn away in that stream; Shakespeare had not.
